exercises.statement: Which of the following expressions correctly describes GDP measured using the expenditure approach?
options: Consumption + investment + government spending + exports − imports
Wages + profits + taxes on production − subsidies + imports
Consumption + investment + government spending + exports + imports
Gross output of all firms, including intermediate consumption
option_explanations: Correct: expenditure-approach GDP = C + I + G + (X − M); imports are subtracted because they are produced abroad.
Incorrect: it mixes the income approach (wages, profits, taxes less subsidies) with imports, which are not domestic income.
Incorrect: imports must be subtracted, not added, since they are produced abroad.
Incorrect: including intermediate consumption double counts; the output approach adds up value added only.
exercises.explanation: Under the expenditure approach, GDP = C + I + G + (X − M): final spending by households, firms and government, plus net exports. Imports are subtracted because they are produced abroad. Option 2 mixes the income approach (wages, profits, taxes less subsidies) with imports, which have nothing to do with domestic income. Option 3 adds imports instead of subtracting them. Option 4 counts intermediate consumption, which leads to double counting: the output approach only adds up value added (output minus intermediate consumption).
exercises.source_ref: ESA 2010 (Regulation (EU) No 549/2013), GDP at market prices — expenditure approach

exercises.statement: A central bank bulletin states: "Headline inflation fell from 6.1% to 3.4% over the year, while core inflation eased only from 4.8% to 4.2%, mainly because energy prices dropped." Which interpretation is correct?
options: The economy is in deflation, since inflation has fallen sharply.
The fall in headline inflation was driven mainly by volatile components, and underlying price pressures remain significant.
Core inflation is higher than headline inflation, so energy prices must have risen during the year.
Since headline inflation is still above core inflation, food and energy prices are rising faster than other prices.
option_explanations: Incorrect: this confuses disinflation (prices rising more slowly) with deflation (prices falling); headline inflation is still 3.4%.
Correct: headline fell 2.7 points but core only 0.6, so energy drove the decline; core at 4.2% shows persistent pressures.
Incorrect: core above headline at year-end is consistent with falling energy prices, exactly as the bulletin says.
Incorrect: at year-end headline inflation (3.4%) is below core inflation (4.2%), not above it.
exercises.explanation: Option 2 is correct: core inflation excludes volatile items such as energy and food. Headline inflation fell by 2.7 points but core inflation by only 0.6 point, so most of the decline comes from energy; underlying (core) price pressures remain well above a 2% target. Option 1 confuses disinflation (prices still rising, but more slowly) with deflation (prices falling). Option 3 is wrong: core inflation (4.2%) being above headline inflation (3.4%) at the end of the year is consistent with energy prices falling, as the statement says. Option 4 is factually wrong: at the end of the year headline inflation (3.4%) is below core inflation (4.2%), not above it.
exercises.source_ref: Eurostat HICP methodology — headline HICP vs HICP excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco (core inflation)

exercises.statement: In the economy of Westland, nominal GDP rose from €500bn in year 1 to €560bn in year 2. Over the same period, the GDP deflator rose from 100 to 108. Calculate the real GDP growth rate between year 1 and year 2, in %, rounded to two decimal places. Use the exact formula, not the approximation.
exercises.explanation: Nominal growth = 560 / 500 − 1 = 12%. Price growth (deflator) = 108 / 100 − 1 = 8%. Real growth = (1 + 0.12) / (1 + 0.08) − 1 = 1.037037 − 1 ≈ 3.70%. Equivalently, real GDP in year 2 at year-1 prices = 560 / 1.08 ≈ €518.5bn, i.e. +3.70% on €500bn. The approximation 12% − 8% = 4.00% overstates real growth by 0.3 point because rates are high.
exercises.source_ref: GDP deflator = nominal GDP / real GDP × 100 ; real growth = (1 + nominal growth) / (1 + inflation) − 1 (ESA 2010, volume measures)

exercises.front: How is the unemployment rate defined (ILO definition), and what is the "labour force"?
exercises.back:
Unemployment rate = number of unemployed ÷ labour force × 100.
The labour force (population active) = employed + unemployed people.
An unemployed person (ILO) is without work, available to start work and has actively looked for a job.
People who are neither working nor looking (students, retirees, discouraged workers) are "economically inactive" and are excluded from the denominator.
exercises.explanation: A common mistake is to divide the number of unemployed by the total working-age population: that ratio is lower and is not the unemployment rate. The employment rate, by contrast, is employed people ÷ working-age population. Discouraged workers who stop searching leave the labour force, which can lower the unemployment rate without any job creation.
exercises.source_ref: ILO resolution concerning statistics of work, employment and labour underutilisation (19th ICLS, 2013) — definition of unemployment

exercises.statement: An IMF staff report on Eastoria estimates actual real GDP at €1,940bn and potential real GDP at €2,000bn for the current year. Which reading of these figures is correct?
options: The output gap is +3%: the economy is overheating and inflationary pressures are building up.
The output gap is −3.09% of actual GDP: Eastoria is necessarily in recession, since GDP is below potential.
The output gap is −3% of potential GDP: there is spare capacity in the economy and demand-driven inflationary pressure should be weak.
The output gap cannot be calculated without the inflation rate, because potential GDP is measured at current prices.
option_explanations: Incorrect: the sign is wrong; (1,940 − 2,000) ÷ 2,000 = −3%, while a positive gap would signal overheating.
Incorrect: it divides by actual GDP instead of potential, and a recession means falling real GDP, not GDP below potential.
Correct: (1,940 − 2,000) ÷ 2,000 = −3%; output below potential means spare capacity and weak demand-driven inflation.
Incorrect: both figures are real (volume) GDP, so no inflation rate is needed to compute the gap.
exercises.explanation: Output gap = (actual GDP − potential GDP) ÷ potential GDP = (1,940 − 2,000) ÷ 2,000 = −3%. A negative gap means the economy produces less than it could without stoking inflation: there is spare capacity (unused labour and equipment), so demand-driven inflationary pressure is weak. Option 1 gets the sign wrong: a positive gap would signal overheating. Option 2 divides by actual GDP (60 ÷ 1,940 = 3.09%) instead of potential GDP, and confuses a level below potential with a recession, which is defined by falling real GDP (two consecutive quarters of negative growth); an economy can grow while remaining below potential. Option 4 is wrong: both figures are real (volume) GDP, so no inflation rate is needed.
exercises.source_ref: Output gap = (actual GDP − potential GDP) ÷ potential GDP, in % of potential — IMF and OECD definitions ; recession rule of thumb: two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth

exercises.statement: Under the ILO definition, a working-age person without a job who has stopped looking for work because they believe no job is available is counted as unemployed.
exercises.justification: False: to be unemployed in the ILO sense, a person must be without work, available and actively seeking work; a discouraged worker who has stopped searching is classified as inactive (outside the labour force).
exercises.explanation: The ILO definition has three cumulative conditions: no work during the reference week, availability to start within two weeks, and active job search during the previous four weeks (or a job found that starts later). A discouraged worker fails the job-search condition and is therefore outside the labour force. This is why the unemployment rate can fall during a long downturn simply because discouraged people leave the labour force: analysts then also look at the participation rate and the employment rate. In French: chômeur au sens du BIT, inactif, travailleur découragé (halo du chômage).
exercises.source_ref: ILO, Resolution concerning statistics of the economically active population, employment, unemployment and underemployment (13th ICLS, 1982), criteria maintained by the Resolution concerning statistics of work, employment and labour underutilization (19th ICLS, 2013): without work, available, seeking work
